title: Convulsive status epilepticus
subject: neurology
summary: Seizure of 5 minutes or more: benzodiazepine within 5 to 20 minutes (IV lorazepam, IM or buccal midazolam), repeat once, then one second-line IV drug by 20 to 40 minutes (levetiracetam 60 mg/kg, fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg or valproate 40 mg/kg), then anaesthetic infusion with EEG for refractory status.

sections.title: Definition and timeline
items: Convulsive status epilepticus: seizure lasting 5 minutes or more, or recurrent seizures without recovery between them. Long-term neuronal injury becomes likely after about 30 minutes (ILAE).
Timeline (AES 2016): 0 to 5 minutes stabilise; 5 to 20 minutes benzodiazepine; 20 to 40 minutes second-line drug; 40 to 60 minutes refractory treatment.
Focal status with impaired awareness: treat from about 10 minutes.
Consider mimics: functional (dissociative) seizures (about 1 in 10 patients in ESETT), rigors, dystonia, decerebrate posturing.
Non-convulsive status: suspect if consciousness does not recover after convulsions stop, or with fluctuating confusion or subtle twitching; needs EEG.

sections.title: 0 to 5 minutes: stabilise
items: Time the seizure. Airway, oxygen, recovery position; nothing in the mouth. Monitor SpO2, ECG and BP.

Check capillary glucose. If below 60 mg/dL (3.3 mmol/L): adults thiamine 100 mg IV then 50 mL of 50% dextrose IV; children 2 years or older 2 mL/kg of 25% dextrose IV; under 2 years 4 mL/kg of 12.5% dextrose IV.
IV or IO access; send glucose, sodium, calcium, magnesium, CBC, renal and liver function, blood gas, antiseizure drug levels, toxicology and pregnancy test as appropriate.
Pregnant beyond 20 weeks or postpartum: treat as eclampsia with magnesium sulfate (see the eclampsia protocol) alongside the benzodiazepine.

sections.title: 5 to 20 minutes: benzodiazepine
items: Give one of: IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (max 4 mg per dose); IM midazolam 10 mg if over 40 kg or 5 mg if 13 to 40 kg; IV diazepam 0.15 to 0.2 mg/kg (max 10 mg per dose).
No IV access: buccal midazolam (10 mg in adults; age-based dose in children, see Children) or intranasal midazolam, or rectal diazepam 0.2 to 0.5 mg/kg (max 20 mg).
If the seizure continues 5 to 10 minutes after the first dose, give one further dose (count any pre-hospital dose). No more than 2 benzodiazepine doses in total.
Underdosing and delay are the commonest errors: give the full weight-based dose at once.
India: lorazepam injection needs refrigeration and may be unavailable. IM midazolam, the midazolam injection given buccally, or IV diazepam are acceptable alternatives.

sections.title: 20 to 40 minutes: second-line drug (single dose)
items: Seizures continuing after 2 benzodiazepine doses: give one IV drug. Levetiracetam, fosphenytoin and valproate are similarly effective, stopping seizures in about half of patients within 60 minutes (ESETT).
Levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV over 10 minutes (max 4500 mg): few interactions and adverse effects; NICE considers it likely to be the preferred option.

Fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg IV (max 1500 mg PE) at up to 150 mg PE/min, or phenytoin 20 mg/kg IV no faster than 50 mg/min (1 mg/kg/min in children), with ECG and BP monitoring. Avoid in toxin-induced seizures.

Valproate 40 mg/kg IV over 10 minutes (max 3000 mg). Avoid in liver disease, suspected mitochondrial (POLG) or urea cycle disorders, and in pregnancy or women and girls who could become pregnant unless there is no alternative.
If none is available: phenobarbital 15 mg/kg IV single dose; be ready to support breathing and BP.
If the first second-line drug fails, an alternative second-line drug may be tried under expert guidance while preparing for anaesthesia (NICE).

sections.title: 40 minutes onward: refractory status
items: Call ICU and anaesthesia. Intubate and start a continuous anaesthetic infusion, with continuous EEG where available; typically maintain seizure suppression for 24 to 48 hours before weaning.
Midazolam 0.2 mg/kg IV bolus, then 0.05 to 2 mg/kg/h infusion.
Propofol 1 to 2 mg/kg IV bolus, then 20 to 200 mcg/kg/min. Watch for propofol infusion syndrome with high doses for more than 48 hours; avoid prolonged use in young children.
Thiopental 2 to 7 mg/kg IV bolus, then 0.5 to 5 mg/kg/h (hypotension and prolonged sedation common).

Continue maintenance doses of the second-line antiseizure drug. Super-refractory or new-onset refractory status (NORSE): specialist care, consider ketamine and autoimmune encephalitis work-up and treatment.

sections.title: Find and treat the cause
items: Common causes: missed or stopped antiseizure medication, alcohol withdrawal, stroke, CNS infection (meningitis, encephalitis, cerebral malaria), neurocysticercosis and tuberculoma (India), metabolic derangement (sodium, calcium, glucose, uraemia), toxins, eclampsia, autoimmune encephalitis.
CT brain once stable. If fever or meningism: LP after imaging when indicated, and do not delay empirical ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours plus aciclovir 10 mg/kg IV every 8 hours (adult doses).
Isoniazid toxicity (TB treatment, overdose): pyridoxine 1 g IV per gram of isoniazid ingested; if the amount is unknown, 5 g IV (children 70 mg/kg, max 5 g).
Urgent EEG if the patient is not returning to baseline, to exclude non-convulsive status.

sections.title: Children
items: Use the same weight-based doses and timeline. Buccal midazolam: 3 to 11 months 2.5 mg; 1 to 4 years 5 mg; 5 to 9 years 7.5 mg; 10 years and over 10 mg.
Febrile status is common in young children: treat the seizure first, then look for meningitis or encephalitis.
Infants with refractory seizures and no clear cause: consider pyridoxine 100 mg IV for pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy.
Valproate carries a higher risk of liver toxicity in children under 2 years and in suspected metabolic disease; prefer levetiracetam.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Waiting for IV access or giving small repeated benzodiazepine doses; giving more than 2 doses (respiratory depression without extra benefit).
Escalating to intubation for functional seizures, or missing non-convulsive status after convulsions stop.
Forgetting glucose and thiamine, or eclampsia in a pregnant or postpartum woman.
Using phenytoin for toxin-induced or alcohol withdrawal seizures.
Stopping an anaesthetic infusion without a maintenance antiseizure drug in place.

drugs.name: Lorazepam
drugs.dose: 0.1 mg/kg IV (max 4 mg per dose), may repeat once after 5 to 10 minutes
drugs.notes: First line in hospital. Store refrigerated.

drugs.name: Midazolam (first line, no IV access)
drugs.dose: IM 10 mg if over 40 kg, 5 mg if 13 to 40 kg, single dose; buccal 10 mg in adults (children by age band)
drugs.notes: Level A equivalent to IV lorazepam (IM route).

drugs.name: Diazepam
drugs.dose: IV 0.15 to 0.2 mg/kg (max 10 mg per dose), may repeat once; rectal 0.2 to 0.5 mg/kg (max 20 mg)

drugs.name: Levetiracetam
drugs.dose: 60 mg/kg IV over 10 minutes (max 4500 mg), single dose
drugs.notes: Second line. Adjust maintenance dose in renal impairment.

drugs.name: Fosphenytoin or phenytoin
drugs.dose: Fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg IV (max 1500 mg PE) at up to 150 mg PE/min; phenytoin 20 mg/kg IV at no more than 50 mg/min (children 1 mg/kg/min)
drugs.notes: Cardiac monitoring: hypotension, arrhythmia. Phenytoin extravasation injury.

drugs.name: Sodium valproate
drugs.dose: 40 mg/kg IV over 10 minutes (max 3000 mg), single dose
drugs.notes: Avoid in liver or mitochondrial disease, under 2 years, pregnancy and women of childbearing potential.

drugs.name: Phenobarbital
drugs.notes: If other second-line drugs are unavailable, or third line. Respiratory depression.

drugs.name: Midazolam infusion
drugs.dose: 0.2 mg/kg IV bolus, then 0.05 to 2 mg/kg/h

drugs.name: Propofol
drugs.dose: 1 to 2 mg/kg IV bolus, then 20 to 200 mcg/kg/min
drugs.notes: Refractory status. Propofol infusion syndrome risk with prolonged high doses.

drugs.name: Thiopental
drugs.dose: 2 to 7 mg/kg IV bolus, then 0.5 to 5 mg/kg/h
drugs.notes: Refractory status. Hypotension; long context-sensitive half-life.
